summary.text: Plastics are synthetic or semisynthetic materials made primarily of polymers that can be molded, extruded or pressed into many solid forms.
They are used around the world because they combine low weight, durability, flexibility, chemical resistance, low toxicity and low-cost production.
Packaging makes up about 40% of their use, but plastics also raise environmental concerns because they decompose slowly in natural ecosystems.

facts.label: First synthetic
facts.value: Bakelite, invented in 1907 by Leo Baekeland

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Ancient Greek for capable of being shaped or molded

items.prompt: Why do manufacturers value the property that gives plastics their name?

options.label: It lets them dissolve into any liquid
It lets them be molded, extruded or pressed into many forms
It lets them stay rigid in every condition
It lets them be made only from petroleum

items.explain: Plasticity allows molding, extrusion or compression into a variety of shapes such as films, fibers, plates, tubes, bottles and boxes.

items.prompt: A plastic cup can be melted down and remolded again and again without any change in its chemical makeup. What kind of plastic is it?

options.label: A thermoplastic
A conductive polymer
A biodegradable plastic
An elastomer

items.explain: Thermoplastics do not undergo chemical change in composition when heated, so they can be molded repeatedly.

items.prompt: How do manufacturers customize the properties of a plastic?

options.label: By shortening every backbone to a single repeat unit
By replacing the monomers with finished polymer chains
By attaching different molecular groups called side chains to the backbone
By removing the backbone from each chain

items.explain: Different molecular groups called side chains hang from the backbone, and their structure influences the properties of the polymer.

items.prompt: Which statement is true of all the plastic discarded so far?

options.label: More than half has been recycled
More has been recycled than incinerated
None of it has been incinerated
More has been incinerated than recycled

items.explain: About 14% has been incinerated and less than 10% recycled.

items.prompt: What is the usual structure of the polymers in most plastics?

options.label: Long chains of repeating units, mostly carbon atoms
Single large crystals of one repeating atom
Rings of oxygen with no carbon in them
Loose mixtures of small separate molecules

items.explain: Most plastics contain organic polymers, mostly chains of carbon atoms with repeating units formed from monomers.

items.prompt: A company says its plastic is made from polylactic acid. Where does it fit in plastic production?

options.label: It is the main route, since most plastic is renewable
It belongs to a growing minority made from renewable resources
It cannot be plastic, since plastics are all petroleum
It is a natural polymer, so it counts as no plastic

items.explain: Most plastics are produced from natural gas and petroleum, but a growing minority come from renewable resources like polylactic acid.

paragraphs.heading: Materials that take any shape
paragraphs.text: Plastics are synthetic or semisynthetic materials made mainly of polymers. What defines them is plasticity: they can be molded, extruded or pressed into many solid shapes, such as films, fibres, tubes, bottles and boxes. The word comes from the Ancient Greek plastikos, meaning able to be shaped or molded. Today it usually means solid synthetic products made from petrochemicals.

paragraphs.heading: Why they are everywhere
paragraphs.text: Plastics spread around the world because that shapeability comes with low weight, durability, flexibility, chemical resistance, low toxicity and cheap production. Packaging takes about 40% of plastic, and building and construction about 20%. Polyethylene is widely used for packaging, while polyvinyl chloride (PVC) goes into construction and pipes because it is strong and durable. Most plastics come from natural gas and petroleum, but a growing minority come from renewable resources such as polylactic acid.

paragraphs.heading: Inside a plastic
paragraphs.text: Most plastics contain organic polymers, and nearly all of these are chains of carbon atoms, with or without oxygen, nitrogen or sulfur attached. Each chain holds several thousand repeating units formed from monomers. The backbone is the main path of the chain, linking the repeat units together. Side chains, groups that hang off the backbone, are usually attached to the monomers before those are linked, and their structure shapes the plastic's properties.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting plastics
paragraphs.text: Plastics are usually grouped by the chemistry of their backbone and side chains. They can also be grouped by how they are made, or by physical properties such as hardness, density and heat resistance. One important divide is whether the chemical processes that make them can be reversed. Thermoplastics do not change chemically when heated, so they can be molded again and again.

paragraphs.heading: Bakelite and the pioneers
paragraphs.text: Bakelite, made by Leo Baekeland in New York in 1907, was the world's first fully synthetic plastic, and Baekeland also coined the word plastics. Many chemists have shaped the materials science of plastics. Herman Mark is known as the father of polymer physics, and the Nobel laureate Hermann Staudinger has been called the father of polymer chemistry.

paragraphs.heading: Growth and waste
paragraphs.text: Output has soared: an estimated 9.2 billion metric tons were made between 1950 and 2017, more than half of it since 2004. Preliminary figures put 2023 production alone above 400 million metric tons, and if trends continue yearly output could pass 1.3 billion tons by 2060. Because plastics break down slowly in nature, they raise widespread environmental concerns. Much ends up in landfills or as pollution, and marine plastic pollution creates garbage patches. Of all plastic thrown away so far, about 14% has been burned and under 10% recycled.
